title: Honest bread
hookLine: Guru Nanak squeezes a poor carpenter's bread and it drips milk, a rich man's bread and it drips blood (Janamsakhi tradition)
carry: bread that drips milk, not blood

cards: Two invitations to dinner arrive on the same night. One is from the richest man in town: a big feast, the best food, everyone important there.
The other is from a carpenter down a side street, and dinner is a plain, rough flatbread made from a coarse grain. The choice looks easy. The guest of honor chose the carpenter.
He's Guru Nanak, the first Guru of the Sikhs, and the story is about what's inside a loaf of bread.

teach.b: Guru Nanak lived in Punjab, and Sikhs honor him as the founder of their path. Many stories of his life are kept in the Janamsakhis, life stories told and written down by his followers.
Sikhs treasure them as stories of the Guru, and they're separate from the scripture itself, the Guru Granth Sahib.
On his travels, Guru Nanak comes to the town of Saidpur and stays with a poor carpenter named Bhai Lalo, eating the simple bread Lalo earns with his own hands.

A wealthy official, Malik Bhago, is holding a great feast, and he's offended that the well-known holy man is staying in a carpenter's hut. He demands that Nanak come, and asks why he refused his fine food.
Nanak asks for two pieces of bread: one from Bhago's feast, one from Lalo's kitchen. He holds one in each hand and squeezes.

teach.h: MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.
teach.b: From Lalo's bread, the story says, drips milk. From Bhago's, drips blood. Bread made by honest work, and bread made by squeezing the poor.
Whatever you make of the miracle, the point is plain.
In Sikh teaching, kirat karni, earning an honest living, goes together with vand chhakna, sharing what you have, and naam japna, remembering God.
A line in the Guru Granth Sahib puts it simply: the one who earns by their own work and gives some away has found the path. And Lalo? His name appears in one of Guru Nanak's hymns in the scripture.
The feast is only in the story. The carpenter is in the hymn.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, honest work, alongside sharing and remembering God; the langar, the free kitchen at gurdwaras, shares food with anyone who comes.

o: bread shared only on holy days
bread earned by your own work, without harming anyone
bread blessed by a priest before anyone eats it

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: a poor carpenter who hosts Nanak
a wealthy official with a feast

s: this story is told in the Guru Granth Sahib itself
it's from the Janamsakhis, stories of the Guru's life kept by his followers.
Lalo's name appears in one of Guru Nanak's hymns
the carpenter is remembered in the scripture itself.
kirat karni means giving up all work to pray
it means earning an honest living by your own work.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. the rich official demands to know why you ate a carpenter's rough bread instead of his feast. what do you do?
o: squeeze a piece of each bread
leave the town without a word
games.why: he squeezes both. Lalo's bread drips milk, and Bhago's drips blood: bread earned honestly, and bread squeezed from the poor.

practice: If you have something to eat nearby, bread, fruit, a cup of tea, hold it; if not, think of your last meal.
Think of the hands it passed through, someone who planted it, picked it, carried it, baked it, stocked the shelf, and then of your own hands and the work that paid for it.
Take a slow bite or sip if you can, taste it properly, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: Honest bread. The carpenter's rough bread that, in the story, dripped milk in Guru Nanak's hand, because it was earned without harming anyone.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work, taught alongside sharing and remembering God.

carryVoice: Your line: bread that drips milk, not blood. Honest work, and something left to share. See you tomorrow.
